item.title: Need Help in moving forward in co authoring: Re: Need Help in moving forward in co authoring
item.content:encoded:
Just post in the forums/chatroom that im looking for a co-author?

Well… you'd want to also try to workshop the draft/concept that you have to see if anyone is interested in just reading it to begin with, rather than expecting people to immediately show interest just because you're asking for a co-author.

item.title: additional idea information: Re: additional idea information
item.content:encoded:
If you're having trouble with presenting your concept concisely, you can look at this thread for tips: http://www.scpwiki.com/forum/t-13369776/how-do-i-remain-brief-when-writing-an-scp-concept

Is it okay if I reply to my Idea post with extra information about the concept?

No. Per the Site Rules, you should avoid replying to your own comments, as that generates spam. Furthermore, reviewers should only have to read at maximum 400 words to understand the basics of your core concept. If you attempt to require reviewers to read more than that when they'd already be doing you the favor of assisting with your writing, you may find that fewer people will be willing to review for you in the first place.

item.title: additional idea information: Re: additional idea information
item.content:encoded:
Really, the 400 word limit exists for a reason. There's no explicit rule about adding onto the original post with a reply, but frankly, that is because it should be common sense not to do so.

Speaking as a reviewer and forum crit staff, the word limit is there to make our lives easier, but I think it can be beneficial to the author, too. When writing an SCP, you are essentially writing a story, forced into a specific format. I think the ideas template can be your first experience with this idea of restriction. It helps you think about your idea in all different aspects aside from what makes it good, which can help you identify flaws. Moreover to the point, the word limit can serve as a gauge for how much you understand an idea.

It's not an exaggeration to say that every single article on the site can be summarized in 400 words or less. It ultimately depends on how you choose to summarize it. Focusing on important aspects, such as structure, narrative, emotion, and so on, while ignoring extraneous details is the best way of summarizing an idea. A reviewer won't care whether your SCP is blue or red, they'll care about the story you're trying to tell, and how you're trying to tell it. Having the ability to summarize your idea in a limited wordspace displays a good understanding of your concept. Believe me when I say that 400 words is actually very generous, in the grand scheme of things.

TL;DR, don't try to artificially decrease word count, save space by booting extraneous details and semantics, make reviewers happy. Good luck!

item.title: Formatting help: Re: Formatting help
item.content:encoded:
I'd also like to point out that you have one too many open brackets at the beginning of the component code. The whole tool won't work unless the excess bracket is excised. Example:

Original:

 [[[include :smlt:component:aers:classification-stuff |item=6000 |lvl=4 |class=Safe |threat=Yellow |threat-colour=#j01 ]]

Updated:

 [[include :smlt:component:aers:classification-stuff |item= $item |lvl= $lvl |class= $class |threat= $threat |threat-colour= $colour ]]

And, yeah, going off of what Croq said, the color hex to turn the dot yellow would be #ffff00.

item.title: Formatting help: Re: Formatting help
item.content:encoded:
The threat colour, #j01 (aka #J01, aka #JJ0011), is a HTML colour hex code. You can change the colour by looking up the hex code of the colour you want. There are also several (140) named HTML colours like "red", "yellow", "gold" that you can look up that will probably also work in this component.

Noting that #JJ0011 isn't a valid HTML colour, so I'd imagine the colour you have there doesn't work currently.

item.title: would a Chernobyl SCP work?: Re: would a Chernobyl SCP work?
item.content:encoded:
would an SCP based on Chernobyl work nowadays?

Technically yes: http://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/scp-4426 "SCP-4426 is the designation for a series of biological masses, located in and around the Chernobyl nuclear power plant and the nearby town of Pripyat."

We also have: http://www.scp-wiki.wikidot.com/scp-3204

So far as writing another Chernobyl SCP goes… not super likely to do well unless you have something extremely unique and unpredictable. There have been a lot of attempts at writing Chernobyl-based anomalies over the years; a forum-only search for "Chernobyl" will probably turn up plenty of concept and draft critique threads.
